question:
Select the most appropriate synonym to substitute the bracketed word in the given sentence.

Confession had always rested on a clear distinction between mortal and (venial) sins.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Pardonable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Venial means slight, minor and easily forgiven or excused; in Christian theology a venial sin is one that can be pardoned, as opposed to a *mortal* sin. (क्षम्य, मामूली)

◦ Pardonable means able to be forgiven or excused — an exact match for "venial". (क्षमा योग्य)

◦ The sentence contrasts "mortal" (deadly, unforgivable) with "venial", so the blank word must mean the opposite of mortal.

◦ Correct: Confession had always rested on a clear distinction between mortal and pardonable sins.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Genial means friendly and cheerful (मिलनसार) — it sounds like "venial" but is unrelated in meaning.

• Major means great or important; it is closer to "mortal" and destroys the contrast.

• Intolerable means unbearable (असहनीय) — the opposite of pardonable.

NOTE

• Synonyms of venial: excusable, forgivable, minor, trivial, slight.

• Antonyms of venial: mortal, unforgivable, inexcusable, grave, heinous.

• Do not confuse venial (pardonable) with venal (corrupt, open to bribery).

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

Sam knew who those people were; the figure in front was ______ his cousin.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. unmistakeably.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs an adverb to modify the sentence — "the figure in front was ______ his cousin" means it was beyond any doubt his cousin. (निस्संदेह)

◦ Unmistakeably/unmistakably = so clear that there can be no mistake; it fits the first clause "Sam knew who those people were".

◦ Correct: Sam knew who those people were; the figure in front was unmistakeably his cousin.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "by mistake" means accidentally/in error — it reverses the intended sense of certainty.

• "at mistake" is not a valid English collocation; the correct phrase is *by mistake*.

• "mistaken of" is ungrammatical; the correct forms are *mistaken for* or *mistaken about*.

NOTE

• Useful certainty adverbs: undoubtedly, unquestionably, undeniably, indisputably, definitely.

• Fixed phrases with mistake: make a mistake, by mistake, mistake A for B.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Insigt.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is Insight — in + sight — meaning a deep understanding of a person or thing. (अंतर्दृष्टि)

◦ The printed word "Insigt" drops the silent h, so it is misspelt.

◦ Correct: The report offers valuable insight into consumer behaviour.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Supply (आपूर्ति) is correctly spelt — noun/verb meaning to provide.

• Optical (दृष्टि संबंधी) is correctly spelt — relating to sight or light.

• Cares (परवाह करता है) is correctly spelt — third person singular of "care".

NOTE

• Words with silent gh: sight, night, height, weight, thought, brought.

• Commonly misspelt SSC words: accommodation, occurrence, embarrass, maintenance, privilege, foreign.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

Rapid climate warming in / the tundra biome have been linked / to increasing shrub dominance.
option_3: the tundra biome have been linked
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. the tundra biome have been linked.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The real subject of the sentence is "Rapid climate warming", which is singular, so the verb must be has been linked, not "have been linked". (कर्ता-क्रिया समन्वय)

◦ "in the tundra biome" is a prepositional phrase; the noun inside a prepositional phrase never controls the verb — this is the rule of proximity trap.

◦ Correct: Rapid climate warming in the tundra biome has been linked to increasing shrub dominance.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "No error" is wrong because the sentence does contain a subject–verb agreement error.

• Option 2 "Rapid climate warming in" is correct — a singular uncountable subject with a preposition.

• Option 4 "to increasing shrub dominance" is correct — "link to" is the right preposition and "increasing" is a participial adjective.

NOTE

• Ignore words between the subject and verb: *The box of chocolates is on the table.*

• Similar structures: *A list of items has been sent.* / *The quality of the mangoes was poor.*

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

Farms are increasingly turning to automation for ______ reasons.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. many.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Reasons" is a plural countable noun, and the determiner used before plural countable nouns to show a large number is many. (अनेक)

◦ Much and little are used only with uncountable nouns (much water, little milk), so they cannot qualify "reasons".

◦ Correct: Farms are increasingly turning to automation for many reasons.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "most reasons" would mean *the majority of a known set of reasons*, which the sentence has not introduced — it is contextually wrong here.

• "much reasons" is ungrammatical because *much* never precedes a plural countable noun.

• "little reasons" is ungrammatical for the same reason; the countable form would be *few reasons*, which reverses the meaning.

NOTE

• Countable → many, few, a few, fewer, number of. Uncountable → much, little, a little, less, amount of.

• *Fewer* + countable (fewer cars) vs *less* + uncountable (less traffic).

question:
Select the appropriate synonym for the underlined word.

I didn't have time to give them proof.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. evidence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Proof means facts or information that establish that something is true. (प्रमाण, सबूत)

◦ Evidence carries the same meaning — the body of facts that supports a conclusion, so it is the closest synonym.

◦ Correct: I didn't have time to give them evidence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Guess means an estimate made without sure information (अनुमान) — the opposite of proof.

• Snap means a sudden sharp sound, a quick photograph, or to break suddenly (चटकना) — unrelated.

• Charge means an accusation, a price, or to load (आरोप/शुल्क) — an accusation is what proof is needed for, not proof itself.

NOTE

• Synonyms of proof: evidence, confirmation, verification, testimony, corroboration, substantiation.

• Related legal collocations: burden of proof, conclusive evidence, circumstantial evidence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Participate in a mock interview to prepare for ______ on your feet and formulating answers under pressure.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. thinking.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to think on your feet" means to react and make decisions quickly and effectively without prior preparation. (तुरंत सोचकर निर्णय लेना)

◦ It pairs naturally with "formulating answers under pressure", which is exactly what a mock interview trains.

◦ The preposition "for" requires a gerund, and "thinking" is the gerund form.

◦ Correct: Participate in a mock interview to prepare for thinking on your feet and formulating answers under pressure.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "blocking on your feet" is not an English idiom and gives no sensible meaning.

• "cursing on your feet" is meaningless and contradicts the professional context of an interview.

• "building on your feet" is not an idiom; the existing idiom is *build on something* (to develop further).

NOTE

• Related "feet" idioms: stand on one's own feet (be independent), get cold feet (lose nerve), find one's feet (settle in), drag one's feet (delay).

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

She blew out the candle and gone to sleepy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. went to sleep.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The first verb "blew" is in the simple past tense, so the verb joined by "and" must also be in the simple past — hence went, not "gone". (समानांतर काल)

◦ "Gone" is the past participle (V3) and cannot stand alone without an auxiliary such as *has/have/had*.

◦ The fixed phrase is go to sleep (noun "sleep"), never "go to sleepy" — *sleepy* is an adjective.

◦ Correct: She blew out the candle and went to sleep.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "went to sleeps" wrongly pluralises the uncountable noun "sleep".

• "go to sleep" is the present/base form and breaks tense parallelism with "blew".

• "No improvement" is wrong because the printed part "gone to sleepy" has both a tense error and a word-form error.

NOTE

• Parallelism rule: verbs joined by *and/or/but* must share the same tense and form — *He came, saw and conquered.*

• V1–V2–V3: go – went – gone; blow – blew – blown; sleep – slept – slept.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

At all costs
option_2: Whatever is needed to achieve something
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Whatever is needed to achieve something.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "at all costs" means regardless of the price, effort or sacrifice involved — no matter what it takes. (हर हाल में, किसी भी कीमत पर)

◦ It is used to stress absolute determination: *We must avoid a leak at all costs.*

◦ Correct: The team was determined to win the final at all costs.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "Not to be trifled with" describes a person who must be taken seriously — that is the idiom *not to be trifled with*, not *at all costs*.

• "To be master of" means to have complete command over something — unrelated to cost or sacrifice.

• "An expensive purchase" is a literal reading of the word "cost" and misses the idiomatic sense.

NOTE

• Similar idioms: by hook or by crook, come what may, at any price, move heaven and earth.

• Note the contrast: at all costs (determination) vs at cost (at the price paid, without profit).

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

Tax dispute settlement might not work out in the desired scale.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. might not work out in.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed collocation is "on a/the scale", not "in the scale" — we always say *on a large scale*, *on a national scale*, *on the desired scale*. (पैमाने पर)

◦ So the preposition in in the segment "might not work out in" must be replaced by on.

◦ Correct: Tax dispute settlement might not work out on the desired scale.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "the desired scale." is correct — the definite article with a past-participle adjective is fine.

• Option 3 "Tax dispute settlement" is a correct noun phrase acting as the subject.

• Option 4 "No error" is wrong because the sentence does contain a preposition error.

NOTE

• Prepositions with "scale": on a large/small/global scale, to scale, scale of 1 to 10.

• Other tested collocations: on purpose, on time, in time, at length, by chance, in vain.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

A unit to measure light
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Lumen.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A lumen (lm) is the SI unit of luminous flux, i.e. the measure of the total visible light emitted by a source. (प्रकाश मापने की इकाई)

◦ Bulb packaging states brightness in lumens, which is why "a unit to measure light" = lumen.

◦ Correct: A unit to measure light is called a lumen.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Watt is the unit of power (rate of energy use), not of light output.

• Horse-power is a non-SI unit of power, chiefly used for engines (1 hp ≈ 746 W).

• Ampere is the SI unit of electric current.

NOTE

• Light-related units: lumen (luminous flux), lux (illuminance = lumen/m²), candela (luminous intensity), candle power.

• Other one-word substitutions: Ammeter (measures current), Barometer (pressure), Seismograph (earthquakes), Hygrometer (humidity).

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

Cell phones keeps loved ones and those nearly them well connected.
option_4: keep loved ones and those near
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. keep loved ones and those near.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject "Cell phones" is plural, so the verb must be the plural form keep, not "keeps". (कर्ता-क्रिया समन्वय)

◦ "Nearly" is an adverb meaning *almost*; what is required here is the adjective/preposition near, meaning *close by* — "those near them".

◦ Correct: Cell phones keep loved ones and those near them well connected.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "No improvement" is wrong because the printed part has both a verb-agreement error and a wrong word form.

• Option 2 "keeping loved and nearly" leaves the sentence without a finite verb and keeps the wrong word "nearly".

• Option 3 "kept love and near" shifts to the past tense unnecessarily and replaces the noun phrase "loved ones" with "love".

NOTE

• Adjective vs adverb pairs: near/nearly, hard/hardly, late/lately, high/highly — the -ly form usually has a different meaning.

• *He works hard* (with effort) vs *He hardly works* (almost not at all).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

Discreet
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Open.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Discreet means careful and prudent in speech or action so as to avoid attention or giving offence — i.e. secretive, tactful, unobtrusive. (विवेकपूर्ण, गुप्त)

◦ Its opposite is being open — frank, public and holding nothing back. (खुला, स्पष्टवादी)

◦ Correct: She was discreet about the news, whereas her brother was completely open about it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Release means to set free or let go (मुक्त करना) — it is not related to discretion.

• Zenith means the highest point or peak (शिखर); its antonym is *nadir*.

• Lose means to fail to keep or win (खोना); its antonym is *find/win*.

NOTE

• Synonyms of discreet: tactful, prudent, circumspect, cautious, guarded.

• Antonyms of discreet: indiscreet, open, blatant, careless, tactless.

• Do not confuse discreet (tactful) with discrete (separate, distinct).

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

He had moved about two inches when several things happened in very ______ succession.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. quick.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The standard collocation is "in quick succession", meaning one event following another rapidly, with very little gap. (तेजी से एक के बाद एक)

◦ The context — "several things happened" while he moved only two inches — demands the idea of speed, which "quick" supplies.

◦ Correct: He had moved about two inches when several things happened in very quick succession.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "brief succession" is not an accepted collocation; *brief* describes duration, not the gap between repeated events.

• "desperate" means hopeless or reckless (हताश) and does not describe a sequence of events.

• "absurd" means ridiculous or illogical (बेतुका) and does not fit the neutral narrative tone.

NOTE

• Fixed collocations with succession: in quick succession, in rapid succession, in close succession.

• Other set phrases: in short supply, in high demand, in full swing, in due course.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

Rolling in cash
option_1: Have a large quantity of money
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Have a large quantity of money.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "rolling in cash" (also *rolling in money/dough/it*) means to be extremely rich, to have plenty of money. (बहुत धनवान होना)

◦ The image is of someone with so much money that he could roll about in it.

◦ Correct: After the company was sold, the founders were rolling in cash.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "A business magnate" names a *person* (a tycoon); the idiom describes a state of wealth, not an occupation.

• "Buying things on interest" refers to credit purchases and has no link with the idiom.

• "To borrow a costly attire" is a literal, unrelated meaning invented as a distractor.

NOTE

• Similar wealth idioms: born with a silver spoon in one's mouth, make a killing, loaded, live in the lap of luxury.

• Poverty idioms often paired in exams: hand to mouth, on the breadline, tighten one's belt.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

Destruction of a fetus
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Feticide.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Feticide (foeticide) literally means the killing or destruction of a fetus — from Latin *fetus* + *-cide* (to kill). (भ्रूण हत्या)

◦ The suffix -cide always denotes an act of killing, e.g. *homicide*, *suicide*, *genocide*.

◦ Correct: The law strictly punishes female feticide.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Fratricide is the killing of one's own brother (भ्रातृहत्या).

• Ellipse is a geometrical figure — an oval closed curve; it has nothing to do with killing.

• Abhor is a verb meaning to hate or detest intensely (घृणा करना), not a one-word substitution for a killing.

NOTE

• Common *-cide* words: matricide (mother), patricide (father), infanticide (infant), regicide (king), uxoricide (wife), genocide (a race), germicide (germs), insecticide (insects).

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

The benefits of rebuilding healthy, fertile soil are clear.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject is "The benefits" (plural), so the plural verb are is correct — the intervening phrase "of rebuilding healthy, fertile soil" does not affect agreement. (कर्ता-क्रिया समन्वय)

◦ Rebuilding is a gerund correctly placed after the preposition "of", and it takes the object "healthy, fertile soil".

◦ "healthy, fertile" are two coordinate adjectives correctly separated by a comma before the noun "soil".

◦ Correct: The benefits of rebuilding healthy, fertile soil are clear. (no change needed)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "healthy, fertile soil" is grammatically sound; *soil* is uncountable and needs no article here.

• Option 2 "The benefits of rebuilding" correctly uses preposition + gerund.

• Option 4 "are clear." correctly matches the plural subject *benefits*.

NOTE

• Rule: the verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, not with the noun nearest to it.

• *The causes of the accident are unknown.* / *The cause of the accidents is unknown.*

question:
Select the appropriate antonym for the underlined word.

The peach-tree is most productive when the roots are kept near the surface.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. futile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Productive means yielding good results, producing plenty — fruitful. (उत्पादक, फलदायी)

◦ Futile means producing no useful result; pointless and unproductive, hence the exact antonym. (व्यर्थ, निष्फल)

◦ Correct: All his efforts to revive the dying peach-tree proved futile.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Lush means growing thickly and luxuriantly (हरा-भरा) — a synonym-side word, not an antonym.

• Potent means powerful and effective (शक्तिशाली) — again close in sense to productive.

• Fertile means capable of producing abundant growth (उपजाऊ) — a direct synonym of productive.

NOTE

• Synonyms of futile: vain, fruitless, useless, ineffective, unavailing, abortive.

• Antonyms of futile: useful, effective, productive, fruitful, worthwhile.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'no substitution required'.

(Beside myself, the only English people) there were Keith and Doreen.
option_1: Besides I, the only English speaking people
option_3: Besides myself, the only English people
option_4: Beside me, the only English people
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Besides myself, the only English people.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Besides means "in addition to / apart from", whereas beside means "by the side of". The sentence lists people in addition to the speaker, so besides is required. (के अलावा बनाम के बगल में)

◦ After "besides" the reflexive/emphatic form myself is idiomatic in this construction, and the rest of the phrase "the only English people" is retained unchanged.

◦ Correct: Besides myself, the only English people there were Keith and Doreen.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Besides I" is wrong because a preposition must be followed by an object pronoun (*me*), not the subject pronoun *I*; it also adds "speaking", changing the meaning.

• Option 2 "No substitution required" is wrong because the printed "Beside" is the wrong word.

• Option 4 keeps the wrong preposition "Beside" (= next to), which makes the sentence illogical.

NOTE

• Beside = at the side of: *He sat beside her.* Besides = in addition to / moreover: *Besides English, she knows French.*

• Idiom: beside oneself (with joy/anger) = extremely upset or excited.

question: Four sentences are given, out of which three have spelling errors. Choose the sentence with all correctly spelt words.
option_1: I don't know weather to eat it or rubb it on.
option_2: Goodbye untill later now, foks. Have a good night.
option_4: Had I known what was coming, I could have prepared myself better.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Had I known what was coming, I could have prepared myself better.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in option 4 — *known, coming, prepared, myself, better* — is spelt correctly, and the inverted conditional (Had I known… I could have prepared) is grammatically sound.

◦ Correct: Had I known what was coming, I could have prepared myself better.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 has rubb (correct: *rub*) and uses weather where the correct word is whether.

• Option 2 has untill (correct: *until*) and foks (correct: *folks*).

• Option 3 has humerous (correct: *humorous*).

NOTE

• Homophone alert: weather (मौसम) vs whether (चाहे/क्या) vs wether (a castrated ram).

• Single vs double letters: *until* (one l), *fulfil/fulfill*, *travelled* (BrE) / *traveled* (AmE), *humorous* (humour → humorous, the *u* is dropped).

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

By the (1) ______ we reach puberty, the world has reached us and (2) ______ us to a greater extent than we realize. (3) ______ family, friends, school, and society in general (4) ______ -by word and example-how to be. But people (5) ______ leaders at that moment when they decide for themselves how to be.

SubQuestion No : 21

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. time.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed conjunctive phrase is "by the time", which introduces a clause meaning *before or when a particular event happens*. (जब तक)

◦ Only "time" collocates with "by the … we reach puberty"; the structure is by the time + subject + verb.

◦ Correct: By the time we reach puberty, the world has reached us…

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "by the moment" is not an English phrase; the accepted forms are *at the moment* and *the moment (that)*.

• "by the age" would need a number — *by the age of twelve* — not a clause.

• "by the era" is unidiomatic; *era* denotes a long historical period, not a personal milestone.

NOTE

• Note the tense rule: By the time + present tense → main clause in present perfect/future perfect: *By the time he arrives, we will have finished.*

• Similar time connectors: as soon as, no sooner … than, hardly … when, the moment.

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

By the (1) ______ we reach puberty, the world has reached us and (2) ______ us to a greater extent than we realize. (3) ______ family, friends, school, and society in general (4) ______ -by word and example-how to be. But people (5) ______ leaders at that moment when they decide for themselves how to be.

SubQuestion No : 22

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. shaped.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The clause reads "the world has reached us and (2) ______ us" — the auxiliary has is shared by both verbs, so the blank needs the past participle (V3): *has reached and (has) shaped*. (वर्तमान पूर्ण काल)

◦ Shape here means to influence or mould a person's character, which fits "to a greater extent than we realize".

◦ Correct: …the world has reached us and shaped us to a greater extent than we realize.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "shapes" is a present-tense form and cannot follow the auxiliary *has*, breaking parallelism with "reached".

• "contours" is chiefly a noun (outlines); as a verb it is rare and would still need the -ed form here.

• "formats" means arranges in a particular layout — wrong in form (present tense) and wrong in sense for human character.

NOTE

• Parallel verbs after one auxiliary must all be V3: *She has sung and danced.*

• Collocations with shape: shape one's future, shape public opinion, take shape, in good shape.

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

By the (1) ______ we reach puberty, the world has reached us and (2) ______ us to a greater extent than we realize. (3) ______ family, friends, school, and society in general (4) ______ -by word and example-how to be. But people (5) ______ leaders at that moment when they decide for themselves how to be.

SubQuestion No : 23

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Our.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage is written in the first person plural — "we reach puberty", "reached us", "than we realize" — so the possessive adjective must agree: Our family, friends, school…

◦ A possessive adjective (my, our, your, his, her, their) is required before the noun "family".

◦ Correct: Our family, friends, school, and society in general have told us…

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• "Their" shifts the person from *we/us* to a third party, destroying the pronoun consistency.

• "Her" is singular and third person, again inconsistent with "we/us".

• "There" is an adverb/introductory word, not a possessive adjective, so it cannot modify "family".

NOTE

• Homophone trap: their (possessive) / there (place) / they're (they are).

• Pronoun consistency: keep the same person throughout — *One must do one's duty*, not *their duty* in formal usage.

In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

By the (1) ______ we reach puberty, the world has reached us and (2) ______ us to a greater extent than we realize. (3) ______ family, friends, school, and society in general (4) ______ -by word and example-how to be. But people (5) ______ leaders at that moment when they decide for themselves how to be.

SubQuestion No : 24

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. have told us.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject is a compound plural — "family, friends, school, and society in general" — so the plural auxiliary have is required. (कर्ता-क्रिया समन्वय)

◦ After *have*, the verb must be the past participle (V3) — told, giving the present perfect *have told*.

◦ "Tell" takes two objects: *tell us how to be* — the structure needs the active voice.

◦ Correct: Our family, friends, school, and society in general have told us — by word and example — how to be.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "have tell us" is wrong because *tell* (V1) cannot follow the auxiliary *have*.

• "has told us" uses a singular auxiliary with a plural compound subject.

• "have been told us" is a passive form; the subject here is the one doing the telling, and a passive cannot keep the object "us".

NOTE

• Subjects joined by and take a plural verb: *Ram and Shyam are friends.*

• V1–V2–V3: tell – told – told; teach – taught – taught; think – thought – thought.

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

By the (1) ______ we reach puberty, the world has reached us and (2) ______ us to a greater extent than we realize. (3) ______ family, friends, school, and society in general (4) ______ -by word and example-how to be. But people (5) ______ leaders at that moment when they decide for themselves how to be.

SubQuestion No : 25

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. begin to become.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subordinate clause uses the simple present — "when they decide for themselves" — so the main verb must also be simple present: begin. (काल की एकरूपता)

◦ After "begin", the to-infinitive takes the base form become, never the past form "became".

◦ Correct: But people begin to become leaders at that moment when they decide for themselves how to be.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "onset to became" is wrong on both counts — *onset* is a noun (beginning), and *became* cannot follow *to*.

• "began to become" is past tense and clashes with the present-tense clause "when they decide".

• "start to became" wrongly puts the past form *became* after the infinitive marker *to*.

NOTE

• Rule: to + V1 always (to go, to become), except in the phrase *used to*, *look forward to*, *object to* where *to* is a preposition and takes V-ing.

• *Begin/start* can take either the infinitive or the gerund: *begin to work* = *begin working*.
